query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the Al content in a CoCrFeNiMn-based HEA will shift the oxidation mechanism toward the formation of a dense, continuous Al2O3 scale that suppresses sub-surface oxidation and porosity, resulting in logarithmic oxidation kinetics and lower overall oxide thickness relative to a low-Al variant.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn-based HEA produced by mechanical alloying, initially containing a lower Al content (e.g., Mn15Al5 composition).
generation.intervention: Systematically increase the Al content (e.g., developing variants such as Mn10Al10 and Mn5Al15) while keeping other parameters constant.
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidation at 800 °C in air for 100 hours.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a thin (<1 μm), dense, and adherent alumina layer that acts as an effective diffusion barrier.
generation.mechanism: A higher Al content facilitates preferential oxidation to form stable Al2O3, which suppresses rapid oxide growth and mitigates sub-surface oxidation and porosity. The protective alumina scale leads to a transition from parabolic to logarithmic kinetics.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with higher Al content will show cumulative mass gains of less than 5 g/m2 and develop oxide layers with thickness around 1 μm, compared to thicker (≈25 μm) and more porous oxides in the low-Al baseline alloy.
generation.baseline: A low-Al CoCrFeNiMn-based HEA (e.g., Mn15Al5 composition) displaying parabolic oxidation kinetics with thick, porous oxide layers.
generation.boundary: Valid for mechanically alloyed CoCrFeNiMn-based HEAs oxidized at around 800 °C in air; limited if the Al addition induces secondary phase formation that interferes with oxidation behaviour.
generation.uncertainty: The exact threshold Al concentration for optimal protective scale formation and potential interactions with other alloying elements that might alter diffusion dynamics.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of CoCrFeNiMn-based HEAs: one with low Al content (e.g., 5 at.%) and one with high Al content (e.g., 15 at.%). Expose both to oxidation at 800 °C in air for 100 hours.
measurements: Cross-sectional SEM/TEM for oxide layer thickness and porosity
XRD to confirm the presence of Al2O3 in the high-Al variant
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-Al alloy fails to form a thinner, continuous Al2O3-dominated oxide scale and does not exhibit significantly lower oxidation kinetics than the low-Al baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.3. Thermal Stability and High-Temperature Oxidation
cited_evidence.text: The high-temperature oxidation at 800 °C was evaluated based on the weight gains of the initially weighted sample with a defined surface. As one can see in Figure 14, the Mn15Al5 alloy showed a sort of parabolic kinetics of oxidation, which is known for rapid weight gain in a matter of minutes and slowing down over time due to the diffusion-driven character of oxygen transport through the developing oxide layer. However, as the annealing prolonged, the oxidation kinetics showed rather a linear mechanism according to the weight gains, suggesting the poor protective behavior of such layer due to, e.g., cracking or formation of pores within the layer. On the other hand, increasing the Al content resulted in logarithmic kinetics of oxidation, suggesting the creation of a dense protective layer, which did not tend to chip off over the time of annealing. Both the Mn10Al10 and Mn5Al15 alloys gained less than 5 g m−2 of newly formed oxides after 100 h annealing at 800 °C. Similar behavior was also reported in the work of Lyu et al. [], who prepared the CoCrFeNiAlx (x = 0.1, 0.5, 1) alloy using vacuum arc melting, which significantly improved its oxidation resistance from 2 at.% of Al. The

The oxidation kinetics changed according to the content of Al initially from a parabolic (Mn15Al5) to a logarithmic (Mn10Al10 and Mn5Al15) rate, caused by the formation of a protective layer of Al2O3 instead of the MnxOy oxidic layer observed in the case of the first-mentioned alloy. Moreover, the sub-surface oxidation and porosity caused by the Mn diffusion toward the oxide layer were completely suppressed from 10 at.% of Al, reducing the overall thickness of the oxide layer from ≈25 μm (Mn15Al5) down to ≈1 μm. Considering the above-stated, changing the content of Al can be used for precise tailoring of the complex performance of the prepared alloys to achieve desired properties not only at the laboratory but also at elevated temperatures.

papers.title: An oxidation resistant refractory high entropy alloy protected by CrTaO4-based oxide.
papers.system: Refractory high-entropy alloys (e.g., NV1 alloy with elements such as Cr, Ta, Al, Ti, Mo, Nb)
papers.approach: Long-term isothermal oxidation experiments at 1000 °C and 1100 °C (up to 200 h) combined with thermogravimetric analysis, XRD and microstructural/EDS analysis.
papers.findings: At 1100 °C, the alloy developed a protective CrTaO4-based oxide layer (with dispersed Al2O3 and Cr2O3) resulting in a lower mass gain, whereas at 1000 °C the oxide was less protective. The reduction in Ti content promoted the formation of the CrTaO4 layer.
papers.mechanism: A lower Ti content favors selective oxidation that leads to a dense CrTaO4-based oxide, which hinders outward cation diffusion and limits the inward ingress of oxygen, thus providing oxidation resistance.

papers.title: Thermodynamic Insights into the Oxidation Mechanisms of CrMnFeCoNi High-Entropy Alloy Using In Situ X-ray Diffraction.
papers.approach: In situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction in air and vacuum with densitometric analysis and phase evolution tracking.
papers.findings: In air, a graded oxide scale was observed consisting of an outer manganese-rich oxide and an inner chromium-rich oxide. The formation sequence followed the differential diffusion rates of Mn, Cr, Fe, Co, and Ni.
papers.mechanism: The oxidation behavior is governed by differential cation diffusion rates: faster outward diffusion of Mn compared to Cr leads to a layered oxide structure; however, no single protective oxide (e.g., Cr2O3) was conclusively identified, complicating the passivation picture in this system.

papers.title: Oxidation Behavior of Refractory AlNbTiVZr0.25 High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.approach: Isothermal oxidation tests at temperatures from 600 °C to 900 °C with kinetics analysis via TGA, XRD, and SEM characterization.
papers.findings: At lower temperatures (600–700 °C), a two-stage oxidation (initial parabolic then breakaway) was observed, while at 800 °C oxidation became nearly linear and at 900 °C the sample disintegrated. Complex oxides such as TiNb2O7, AlNbO4, and Nb2Zr6O17 were identified, with some oxides (e.g., AlNbO4) linked to slower kinetics.
papers.mechanism: Oxidation is controlled by the formation of multi-component oxide scales with varying protective capability. Certain phases may slow oxidation (as with some Al-containing oxides) while others do not provide an effective barrier.

papers.title: Modeling Oxidation of AlCoCrFeNi High-Entropy Alloy Using Stochastic Cellular Automata.
papers.approach: Mesoscale modeling using a stochastic cellular automata approach integrating thermodynamics, kinetics, and microstructural features (including effects of grain boundaries versus single-crystal behavior).
papers.findings: The simulations predicted initial formation of all oxides, with eventual predominance of α-Al2O3 and Cr2O3 depending on microstructural conditions. The models helped rationalize the oxide scale morphology differences when phase-segregation is present.
papers.mechanism: The oxide growth mechanism is governed by the complex interplay between diffusion (bulk vs. grain boundary), thermodynamic stability of the oxides, and microstructural heterogeneity that dictate which protective scales (like Al2O3 and Cr2O3) form and how they coalesce.

papers.title: Enhanced Oxidation Resistance of Ultrafine-Grain Microstructure AlCoCrFeNi High Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi HEA with ultrafine-grain microstructure (processed via friction processing)
papers.approach: Mechanical processing to refine grain structure, followed by oxidation testing (850–1050 °C for 100 h) and analysis of oxidation kinetics and oxide scale morphology via SEM and cross-sectional studies.
papers.findings: Ultrafine-grained samples showed significant reductions (up to 38–48%) in oxidation kinetics relative to as-cast alloys and developed protective oxide scales predominantly composed of chromia and alumina forming inner layered structures.
papers.mechanism: The increased density of grain boundaries in ultrafine microstructures accelerates controlled internal oxidation, leading to the formation of a continuous protective chromium oxide layer that is subsequently supplemented by an Al-rich inner oxide, thus reducing overall oxygen ingress.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding of speciated oxide growth in high entropy alloys.
papers.approach: Advanced in-situ characterization techniques including atom probe tomography, TEM, and X-ray absorption near-edge structure analysis to study oxidation-induced compositional and structural changes.
papers.findings: Observed that initial oxide formation is influenced by atomic size while prolonged oxidation is dominated by redox potential effects, leading to compositional inversion and hierarchical oxide scale formation.
papers.mechanism: Oxide scale formation is dictated by a competition between kinetic factors (such as element diffusivity) and thermodynamic tendencies (redox potentials and cohesive energies) with speciation evolving over time from non-protective to potentially protective oxides.

papers.title: Influence of the Al Content on the Properties of Mechanically Alloyed CoCrFeNiMnXAl20-X High-Entropy Alloys.
papers.system: CoCrFeNiMn-based HEAs with variable Al content
papers.approach: Systematic variation of Al content in mechanically alloyed HEAs followed by high-temperature oxidation studies at 800 °C with cross-sectional and kinetic analyses.
papers.findings: Alloys with higher Al content (from 10 to 15 at.%) demonstrated logarithmic oxidation kinetics with formation of a dense, protective Al2O3 scale and suppression of sub-surface oxidation, whereas lower Al content alloys exhibited parabolic kinetics with thick, porous oxide layers dominated by manganese oxides.
papers.mechanism: The formation and retention of a protective oxide layer are governed by the availability of Al to form stable Al2O3. Sufficient Al content shifts the oxidation mechanism from a rapidly growing, non-protective MnxOy scale to a dense, adherent alumina layer, preventing deleterious internal oxidation.

papers.title: High Temperature Oxidation Behavior of an Equimolar Cr-Mn-Fe-Co High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: Equimolar Cr-Mn-Fe-Co HEA produced by 3D laser printing
papers.approach: High-temperature oxidation experiments at 700 °C and 900 °C with kinetic measurements, phase identification, and morphological observation.
papers.findings: Oxidation followed parabolic kinetics with the formation of spinel-type oxides; however, at 900 °C, exfoliation of the scale was observed along with the segmentation of the matrix, indicating poor long-term scale adherence.
papers.mechanism: Protection in this alloy is limited by the instability of the spinel oxide scale and the differential diffusion rates leading to Kirkendall void formation, resulting in eventual spallation.

established: Protective oxide layers (e.g., Al2O3, Cr2O3, CrTaO4) can form on HEA surfaces and are key to high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Oxidation kinetics in HEAs are often diffusion-controlled (parabolic behavior) and sensitive to microstructural features such as grain size and phase segregation.
Alloy composition (e.g., Ti reduction, increased Al content) is critical to tailoring the type and stability of the protective oxide scale.
Differential diffusion rates among constituent elements govern the formation and evolution of multi-layered oxide scales.

approaches_tried.approach: Adjusting alloy composition (e.g., reducing Ti, increasing Al content)
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced formation of protective oxides (CrTaO4-based layer or dense Al2O3 scale) which reduce oxidation kinetics.

approaches_tried.approach: Mechanical processing to refine grain microstructure
approaches_tried.outcome: Increased grain boundary density promotes controlled internal oxidation and formation of continuous protective scales, lowering oxidation rates.

approaches_tried.approach: Mesoscale modeling using stochastic cellular automata
approaches_tried.outcome: Clarified the roles of thermodynamics, kinetics, and microstructure in oxide scale formation, predicting the coexistence and segregation of protective oxides.

mechanisms: Selective oxidation driven by compositional tuning (e.g., reduced Ti enhances CrTaO4 formation).
Formation of continuous protective oxide layers by balancing the rates of outward cation diffusion and inward oxygen diffusion.
Grain boundary diffusion effects that accelerate the formation of protective internal oxide layers (e.g., chromia followed by alumina).
Competitive oxidation controlled by elemental diffusivity and redox potential leading to hierarchical oxide scale evolution.
disagreements: The identity of the most protective oxide: some studies emphasize CrTaO4 or Cr2O3 protection, while others highlight the key role of Al2O3.
Discrepancies in the oxide scale structure (continuous versus porous/spalled scales) and the role of specific elements (for example, absence of protective Cr2O3 in some Cantor alloy studies).
Variations in oxidation kinetics (parabolic vs. linear or logarithmic) under similar test conditions, likely due to differences in microstructure and testing duration.
open_questions: What is the precise mechanistic interplay between elemental diffusivities, redox potentials, and microstructural features in forming a continuously protective oxide layer?
How do long-term oxidation exposures (beyond 100–200 hours) influence the integrity and stability of the protective oxide scales in different HEA systems?
Can a single, unifying mechanism be identified that controls protective oxide formation across different HEA compositions and processing conditions?
Under what controlled conditions (e.g., oxygen partial pressure, temperature regimes) do the protective oxides fail or spall?
opportunities: Perform controlled comparative studies by systematically varying a single elemental parameter (e.g., Ti or Al content) to directly correlate composition with protective oxide formation and retention.
Integrate in situ high-temperature characterization techniques (e.g., HTXRD, TEM with heating stages) over extended durations to monitor oxide scale evolution.
Combine mechanical processing with targeted compositional tuning to optimize grain boundary characteristics and diffusion pathways for enhanced scale stability.
Develop advanced modeling frameworks that couple mesoscale simulations with experimental in situ observations to predict oxidation behavior under variable boundary conditions.

directions.direction: Composition design by adjusting critical element content (e.g., reducing Ti and/or increasing Al or Cr) to favor the formation of protective oxides.
directions.assessment: This approach directly targets the element-specific oxidation behavior. Evidence shows that a reduced Ti content promotes a protective CrTaO4-based oxide (e.g. PMC6513993::web::015::discussion) and that higher Al content leads to a dense Al2O3 scale (PMC9692591::web::026::4_conclusions). The physics of selective oxidation and diffusion are well established, making this an actionable and informative intervention.

directions.direction: Microstructure control via grain refinement to enhance grain boundary diffusion and promote a continuous, adherent protective oxide.
directions.assessment: Studies using friction processing to produce ultrafine-grain structures have shown accelerated formation of protective chromium or alumina scales (PMC9026100::web::017::oxidation_kinetics). This mechanism leverages faster GB diffusion to enable uniform oxide scale formation without spallation, making it a directly testable modification.

directions.direction: Oxidation environment control by varying oxygen partial pressure to reveal the role of differential cation diffusion in oxide scale formation.
directions.assessment: Comparative studies under air versus vacuum conditions can decouple the effects of oxygen ingress and cation diffusion (PMC10384371::web::024::4_2_oxidation_in_vacuum; PMC10384371::web::026::4_3_oxidation_in_air). The well-known physics of diffusion under different ambient conditions support this approach, and measurable oxide morphology differences would be highly informative.

directions.direction: In situ real-time high-temperature phase evolution studies combined with modeling to relate kinetic diffusion parameters and thermodynamic driving forces to oxide formation and protective layer retention.
directions.assessment: Mesoscale modeling and in situ HTXRD experiments (PMC9498035::web::005::1_introduction; PMC10384371::web::020::3_3_htxrd_in_air) support the idea that coupling thermodynamic stability with diffusion kinetics governs oxide selection. Although more complex in design, this direction could yield detailed mechanistic insights across various alloy compositions.

candidates.hypothesis: Reducing the concentration of fast-diffusing Ti in a refractory high-entropy alloy will enable selective oxidation of Cr and Ta to form a dense CrTaO4-based oxide layer that significantly retards oxidation at 1100 °C compared to an alloy with higher Ti content.
candidates.intervention: Adjust alloy composition to reduce Ti content by approximately 75% relative to a baseline alloy with higher Ti.

candidates.hypothesis: An ultrafine-grained AlCoCrFeNi HEA processed by friction processing will form and retain a continuous protective oxide (predominantly Cr2O3 with subsequent Al2O3 enrichment) at high temperatures, leading to a 38–48% reduction in oxidation kinetics relative to its as-cast coarse-grained counterpart.
candidates.intervention: Apply stationary friction processing (e.g., 5-minute treatment at 1800 rpm) to refine the grain size to <1 μm.

candidates.hypothesis: Increasing the Al content in a CoCrFeNiMn-based HEA will shift the oxidation mechanism toward the formation of a dense, continuous Al2O3 scale that suppresses sub-surface oxidation and porosity, resulting in logarithmic oxidation kinetics and lower overall oxide thickness relative to a low-Al variant.
candidates.intervention: Systematically increase the Al content (e.g., developing variants such as Mn10Al10 and Mn5Al15) while keeping other parameters constant.

candidates.hypothesis: Under high oxygen partial pressure (ambient air), an equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi HEA will develop a protective oxide scale dominated by Cr-rich components due to differential cation diffusion rates, whereas under low oxygen partial pressure (vacuum conditions) the oxide scale will be non-protective and dominated by Mn-rich oxides, leading to higher oxidation kinetics.
candidates.intervention: Subject identical samples to oxidation tests under two atmospheres: ambient air (1 atm O2) and high vacuum (~4.2×10⁻⁶ atm).
